method: Full-source first pass using preserved HTML/XML records. Each body paragraph, source metadata, exclusions, editorial notes, scholarly material and bibliography was read; conclusions below separate Darwin voice from Caroline/Catherine or other reported voices and preserve date/receipt limits. Candidate links are not accepted.

source_scope.figures: No assigned record supplied an inline visual requiring separate figure interpretation in this pass.

outgoing_reviews.summary: Darwin’s April 3–6 Rio letter is a multipart voyage report: Bahia climate and vegetation, planned Rio residence and inland Fazenda excursion, the bundle of family letters received on April 5, and a planned move to Botofogo. The family material is affectionate and names letters from Catherine and Henslow; it does not identify Caroline’s March 12–31 letter as an input.

This letter was sealed with the prior one and carried through McCormick’s return. Darwin describes the exhausting inland Brazilian expedition, a swamped boat damaging books and instruments, his view of FitzRoy and ship life, and the altered Bahia plan. The April 26 dateline is appended after composition; no Caroline prompt is named.

The October–November multipart account covers the first and planned second cruises, Patagonia and fossil bones, political uncertainty at Monte Video, and a November sequence of received letters. P4 explicitly acknowledges Caroline’s June 28 letter; later blocks list Catherine, Susan and Erasmus letters. The exact Caroline body is the plausible context 173, with a scoped candidate response relationship.

proposed_links.scope: P4 acknowledgment and nearby letter/news discussion
proposed_links.reason: Darwin explicitly says he has received Caroline’s letter of June 28; broader answer scope is not proven.

evidence.quote: I have just received your letter of June 28

outgoing_reviews.summary: Darwin’s March–April journal-letter recounts Cape Horn weather, Tierra del Fuego and the Falklands, fossil shells in ancient rocks, and plans for the Rio Negro. Its dated internal sections and later April continuation are voyage composition layers; it names no specific Caroline input or received letter.

Darwin reports his 500–600 mile ride from Rio Negro through the Colorado to Bahia Blanca, fossil armour and bones, and a planned return to the Beagle. P4 says the Captain enclosed Catherine’s 29 May letter; that Catherine input is not one of the assigned Caroline records, so no Caroline prompt is established.

This letter narrates the 800-mile northern tour, illness at Santa Fe, blockaded Buenos Aires, Covington’s near-drowning and lost gun, financial drafts, and the plan to extract Covington by boat if needed. The journal packet sent through Beaufort is an own-letter/logistical reference, not an incoming Caroline prompt.

Darwin thanks Caroline for a letter dated September 1 and reports that his Buenos Aires troubles ended, geological work continued, specimens were packed, and the schooner and crew plans changed. The date and explicit thanks identify DCP-LETT-214 as a plausible antecedent; the match is scoped to the acknowledgment and general news, not a whole-letter answer.

proposed_links.reason: Darwin explicitly thanks Caroline for a letter dated September 1; the surviving source matches that date, but no distinctive substantive answer establishes whole-letter scope.

evidence.quote: I have to thank you for a letter dated September 1st
We were exceedingly glad to receive your letter last week from Rio Negro dated 12 April

outgoing_reviews.summary: Darwin acknowledges Caroline’s letter dated March 9 and Owen’s long letter, then discusses fossil-numbering and carriage instructions for Clift, a Buenos Aires box for Henslow, finances, and an impending Andes excursion. The March 9 Caroline letter is not DCP-LETT-202 (dated March 7), so the prompt remains unlocated.

Darwin writes while recovering from illness after the Chilean excursion, discusses Cauquenes, the sale of the Adventure and altered voyage plans, and mentions his new correspondent Fox. His thanks to Susan and Catherine concern their own messages; no Caroline letter is identified beyond routine correspondence.

The March 10–13 letter fixes an end to the voyage, gives routing instructions for future mail, describes the February 20 Concepción earthquake and lost anchors, and records a temporary shore stay and travel to Santiago. P6 says only that two letters had arrived, without identifying their writers; no assigned Caroline input is established.

Darwin’s Peru letter resumes a geological travel narrative after three months of missing mail, then records receiving three more English letters through February 1835. It separately notes two affectionate Fox letters and gives new routing instructions. The statements establish delivery intervals but do not identify a Caroline source among this packet.

Darwin describes Tahiti, New Zealand, missionaries, the coming Sydney call and future routing. P9 says he received Caroline’s March letter by an extraordinary chance before leaving the Galapagos, but its date/text is not recovered in the assigned contexts; the later Caroline records are chronologically impossible.

This April 29 letter from the Cocos/Keeling Islands discusses coral-island formation, homesickness, geology and plans for London publication. P7 says the last received letter was thirteen months old and asks Caroline to repeat important news; this is explicit mail deprivation, not evidence that every earlier Caroline letter was inaccessible.

Darwin’s July 18 Ascension-bound letter delays the expected homecoming, reflects on St Helena geology and scenery, and reports that a bundle of letters exists but has not yet been opened. The postscript and cover annotation separate anticipated receipt from actual reading; no Caroline prompt is identified.

After returning to England, Darwin reports intense visits to naturalists, a possible move to Maer, and the Captain’s marriage news. The letter from FitzRoy 312 is the established prior context for the Captain news; Caroline’s plan for Maer has no identified written prompt, and the E. Holland note is only described as civility.

Darwin postpones his departure because plans are unsettled, asks Caroline to arrange the Phaeton if he does not write, and describes unpacked fossil bones including giant ant-eater and rhinoceros-sized heads. His London gossip and Murchison map visit are self-contained; no Caroline incoming is named.

Darwin gives a Clapham and London social diary, reports Fanny and Hensleigh reviewing his Journal, Holland’s advice about overlap with FitzRoy, Lyell’s practical counsel and the fossil bones, then plans Cambridge. It asks no answer and identifies no Caroline prompt.

incoming_reviews.summary: Caroline’s long March family letter reports the Langton wedding, Maer visitors and household gossip, with Marianne Parker’s appended flap. It explicitly says Susan sent a letter to Rio and that the family is waiting for Darwin from Madeira; its date is later than Darwin 164’s receipt of December 31 and February 4 letters, so it cannot be that prompt.

Caroline records delight at Darwin’s St Salvador letter, family visits, gardening and local news, then finishes the letter June 28. Darwin 188 P4 explicitly says he has just received “your letter of June 28”; the dated endpoint and acknowledgment support a candidate scoped reply/receipt relation.

Caroline reports Susan’s dispatched letter, Musters’s death, Erasmus’s books and Fox’s illness, then family health and anticipation of Darwin’s return. The closing date is September 25 despite the catalogue range; no later Darwin target names this particular letter as its prompt.

Caroline explains she is writing because Catherine had not begun her turn, then gives quiet family news, parties and wishes for a happy new year. It contains no distinctive question or request answered by Darwin 203 or later targets.

Caroline congratulates Darwin on collecting, relays Mr Hughes’s news, safeguards the journal, and gives marriage and family updates. Darwin 253 refers instead to a letter dated March 9, while this source is dated March 7; that two-day mismatch prevents treating it as the acknowledged prompt.

This May letter warns that Beaufort expected a long mail gap, supplies Maer and family news, and discusses the orchard, so it is a mail-context record rather than a scientific prompt. Darwin 215’s received Catherine letter is separately identified and does not establish 205.

Caroline’s September letter acknowledges Darwin’s April 12 Rio Negro letter, reports family illness and finances, and notes that Marianne holds Darwin’s letter. Its dated “September 1” identity is explicitly repeated by Darwin 230 P1, making it a candidate antecedent for that limited acknowledgment.

Caroline has read Darwin’s journal and gives concrete criticism about its interest and publication, sends shoes/books and news of Ross, and reports family visits. Darwin 222 does not answer these points; it is a fresh travel and Covington crisis report.

Caroline responds to Darwin’s September 20 Buenos Aires account, discusses his ride and the trade situation, and gives New Year and family news. Darwin 222’s account of a later Buenos Aires crisis does not identify this source as its prompt.

Caroline answers Darwin’s November 13 letter, confirms peace and the fossil-bone arrangements, copies Erasmus’s report of Clift’s delight, and gives family and university news. Darwin 230 predates this source and therefore cannot reply to it; no later assigned target identifies it.

Caroline responds to Darwin’s April 6 Falkland letter with family and household news, confirms the family’s regular monthly writing, and reports the rebuilding of the greenhouse. Darwin 259 follows chronologically but does not acknowledge these distinctive details; topic continuity alone is insufficient.

Caroline acknowledges Darwin’s July letters to Catherine and herself, gives the Liverpool bone-box and Henslow information, and treats the promotion/homecoming report as uncertain. Darwin 271 follows but does not name this source or answer these details.

This joint Caroline/Catherine letter answers Darwin’s October 13 letter by discussing his illness and disappointment about Patagonia; Catherine’s separate paragraph urges him to leave the Beagle. The two hands/voices must remain separate. It is a plausible family response context but no specific assigned Darwin target is a direct answer.

Caroline responds to Darwin’s November 8 letter, noting Corfield’s kindness during illness and Owen’s delighted receipt of Darwin’s letter. Family and political news follow; the source provides receipt evidence for the earlier Darwin letter, not a prompt for a later outgoing target.

Caroline acknowledges Darwin’s July 17 Lima letter, reports the approaching return, family health and Sedgwick’s published discourse, then appends Catherine’s affectionate corner. The appended voices and December 29 date do not identify a later Darwin prompt.

Caroline writes with the family’s expectation of Darwin’s imminent return, mentions Susan and Catherine’s later letters and Erasmus’s house, and says she scarcely expects Darwin to receive this one. It is a late grounding letter with no explicit response target in the assigned outgoing set.

findings.reason: The 313 body says “I have heard from the Captain” and the post-return primary review already treats FitzRoy 312 as the engagement-news context.

findings.finding: 164 P4 records receipt of letters dated December 31 and February 4 on April 5; 163 is a March 12–31 composition and cannot be silently backdated into that receipt.
Caroline and Catherine occupy separate body sections; their illness/return advice must not be collapsed into one authorial voice.
The “last letter I received was 13 months ago” statement is a local mail-gap report, not a universal claim about all family correspondence.
Both outgoing letters identify received dated letters whose surviving Caroline source is absent or date-mismatched; missing inputs remain unlocated.

limitations: This pass does not create accepted relationships or export training material. Candidate links 188→173 and 230→214 need root adjudication.

The source projection supplies full paragraph text and metadata; no assigned inline visual asset was present. Editorial summaries and notes were read as apparatus and excluded from Darwin/Caroline body voice.
